content.what_is_it: Urticaria (commonly known as hives) is a sudden, highly itchy skin reaction characterized by the appearance of raised bumps, swollen plaques (wheals), or both. Individual hives are characteristically evanescent (transient), usually resolving within 24 hours while new hives may continue to erupt on other parts of the body.
content.how_common: Extremely common; millions of individuals experience acute hives during their lifetime. Chronic spontaneous hives affect millions worldwide, occurring twice as often in women (most frequently between ages 20 and 40).
content.chronic_or_acute: Classified into Acute Urticaria (lasting fewer than 6 weeks, commonly resolving in days to weeks) and Chronic Urticaria (occurring daily or almost daily for 6 weeks or longer).
content.histamine_pathophysiology: Mast cells and basophils in the dermis release histamine and other vasoactive mediators. Histamine causes local capillary dilation and fluid leakage into the superficial dermis, leading to localized dermal edema (wheal), erythema, warmth, and intense itching. When fluid extravasates deeper into the subcutaneous or submucosal tissue, angioedema develops.

text:
Condition: Urticaria (Hives)
Section: Overview

What Is It: Urticaria (commonly known as hives) is a sudden, highly itchy skin reaction characterized by the appearance of raised bumps, swollen plaques (wheals), or both. Individual hives are characteristically evanescent (transient), usually resolving within 24 hours while new hives may continue to erupt on other parts of the body.
How Common: Extremely common; millions of individuals experience acute hives during their lifetime. Chronic spontaneous hives affect millions worldwide, occurring twice as often in women (most frequently between ages 20 and 40).
Chronic Or Acute: Classified into Acute Urticaria (lasting fewer than 6 weeks, commonly resolving in days to weeks) and Chronic Urticaria (occurring daily or almost daily for 6 weeks or longer).
Contagious: Not Contagious
Histamine Pathophysiology: Mast cells and basophils in the dermis release histamine and other vasoactive mediators. Histamine causes local capillary dilation and fluid leakage into the superficial dermis, leading to localized dermal edema (wheal), erythema, warmth, and intense itching. When fluid extravasates deeper into the subcutaneous or submucosal tissue, angioedema develops.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)
Page: (AAD)/Hives: Overview
Source URL: https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/a-z/hives-overview

content.description: Smooth, raised spots or large confluence plaques ranging from pinhead size to larger than a dinner plate. They feel intensely itchy, stinging, or burning, and are warm to the touch.
typical_locations: Can appear anywhere on the body, including trunk, arms, legs, face, hands, and feet.

content.lighter_skin_tones: Hives appear as bright pink or distinct red raised welts; severe central edema may appear pale white with a red flare border.
content.darker_skin_tones: Hives often match natural skin tone or appear slightly darker (brown, violaceous) or slightly lighter; redness is often subtle or undetectable; post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (dark spots) can linger after hives resolve.

content.name: Cold Temperature and Cold Exposure (Cold Urticaria)
content.threshold_risk: Sudden drop in ambient temperature, exposure to cold wind, swimming in cold water, or handling ice
content.mechanism: Direct activation of cold-sensitive cutaneous mast cells causing immediate histamine release upon re-warming.
content.prevention_and_action: Wear warm windproof clothing and face scarves in cold weather; avoid sudden immersion in cold bodies of water (severe risk of body-wide reaction); avoid icy drinks.

content.name: Heat, Exercise, and Sweating (Cholinergic Urticaria)
content.threshold_risk: Ambient heat (> 28°C / 82°F), strenuous physical exercise, hot baths, or spicy food causing sweating
content.mechanism: Rise in core body temperature and release of acetylcholine by sweat nerve fibers triggers mast cell degranulation, producing small pinpoint itchy wheals surrounded by large red flares.
content.prevention_and_action: Stay in cool air-conditioned environments during heatwaves; take lukewarm or cool showers; avoid hot tubs and intense workouts in high heat.

source.page_title: (AAD)/Hives: How to get relief at home

itch_relief_and_cooling: Apply a clean, cool, damp washcloth (cool compress) to itchy skin for 10 to 20 minutes to rapidly soothe inflammation and constrict dilated capillaries.
Add colloidal oatmeal to a bathtub of warm (not hot) water and soak for the recommended time on the package.
Apply over-the-counter anti-itch lotion containing pramoxine or calamine as directed.
scratching_and_infection_prevention: Never scratch or vigorously rub itchy hives, as mechanical friction provokes additional histamine release and triggers new wheals (dermatographism).
Keep fingernails trimmed short and clean to prevent scratching excoriations and secondary bacterial infection.
bathing_and_cleansing_hygiene: Take warm (lukewarm) baths or showers—NEVER hot water, as hot water worsens vasodilation and triggers intense itching.
Use only gentle, fragrance-free cleansers applied gently with bare hands; avoid washcloths, loofahs, or abrasive sponges.
Avoid products labeled 'Unscented' (which contain masking fragrances); choose only 'Fragrance-Free'.
clothing_recommendations: Wear loose-fitting, smooth 100% cotton clothing to prevent friction and sweat entrapment.
Avoid tight elastic bands, tight undergarments, and coarse wool fabrics.
symptom_journaling: Keep a daily symptom and food diary noting the exact date/time hives erupted, activities preceding the flare, foods/drinks consumed, medications taken, temperature/sweat exposure, and stress levels.

text:
Condition: Urticaria (Hives)
Section: Skin Care and Self Care

Itch Relief And Cooling:
  - Apply a clean, cool, damp washcloth (cool compress) to itchy skin for 10 to 20 minutes to rapidly soothe inflammation and constrict dilated capillaries.
  - Add colloidal oatmeal to a bathtub of warm (not hot) water and soak for the recommended time on the package.
  - Apply over-the-counter anti-itch lotion containing pramoxine or calamine as directed.
Scratching And Infection Prevention:
  - Never scratch or vigorously rub itchy hives, as mechanical friction provokes additional histamine release and triggers new wheals (dermatographism).
  - Keep fingernails trimmed short and clean to prevent scratching excoriations and secondary bacterial infection.
Bathing And Cleansing Hygiene:
  - Take warm (lukewarm) baths or showers—NEVER hot water, as hot water worsens vasodilation and triggers intense itching.
  - Use only gentle, fragrance-free cleansers applied gently with bare hands; avoid washcloths, loofahs, or abrasive sponges.
  - Avoid products labeled 'Unscented' (which contain masking fragrances); choose only 'Fragrance-Free'.
Clothing Recommendations:
  - Wear loose-fitting, smooth 100% cotton clothing to prevent friction and sweat entrapment.
  - Avoid tight elastic bands, tight undergarments, and coarse wool fabrics.
Symptom Journaling:
  - Keep a daily symptom and food diary noting the exact date/time hives erupted, activities preceding the flare, foods/drinks consumed, medications taken, temperature/sweat exposure, and stress levels.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)
Page: (AAD)/Hives: How to get relief at home
Source URL: https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/a-z/hives-self-care

early_signs_of_flare: Sudden tingling, warmth, or prickling sensation in the skin
Rapid emergence of small red or skin-toned itchy spots
Localized swelling on eyelids, lips, or extremities
immediate_action_plan: Take prescribed second-generation non-sedating H1-antihistamine immediately according to your dermatologist's plan.
Apply cool damp compresses to soothe active itching.
Remove tight clothing and rest in a cool, quiet room.
Monitor immediately for any red flag signs of breathing difficulty or throat swelling.

text:
Condition: Urticaria (Hives)
Section: Flare-Up Management

Early Signs Of Flare:
  - Sudden tingling, warmth, or prickling sensation in the skin
  - Rapid emergence of small red or skin-toned itchy spots
  - Localized swelling on eyelids, lips, or extremities
Immediate Action Plan:
  - Take prescribed second-generation non-sedating H1-antihistamine immediately according to your dermatologist's plan.
  - Apply cool damp compresses to soothe active itching.
  - Remove tight clothing and rest in a cool, quiet room.
  - Monitor immediately for any red flag signs of breathing difficulty or throat swelling.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)

content.sign: Anaphylaxis and Severe Upper Airway Angioedema
content.description: Rapid swelling of the lips, tongue, mouth, or throat; difficulty swallowing (dysphagia); hoarseness; shortness of breath or wheezing (dyspnea); lightheadedness, dizziness, fainting; racing heart rate; nausea or vomiting.

content.action: Administer an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen, Auvi-Q, Adrenaclick) immediately into the outer thigh, call emergency medical services, and proceed directly to an emergency department.

content.details: First-line cornerstone of urticaria therapy. Blocks H1 histamine receptors to reduce itching, wheal formation, and swelling. Under dermatologist supervision, dosages may be safely up-titrated up to 4 times the standard daily dose for refractory chronic hives.

text:
Condition: Urticaria (Hives)
Section: Medications and Treatments
Subsection: First-Line Therapy

Class: Second-Generation H1-Antihistamines (Non-Sedating)
Examples:
  - Cetirizine (Zyrtec)
  - Loratadine (Claritin)
  - Fexofenadine (Allegra)
  - Desloratadine (Clarinex)
  - Levocetirizine (Xyzal)
Details: First-line cornerstone of urticaria therapy. Blocks H1 histamine receptors to reduce itching, wheal formation, and swelling. Under dermatologist supervision, dosages may be safely up-titrated up to 4 times the standard daily dose for refractory chronic hives.
Prescription Status: OTC and Prescription
